# Recommendation: Use `std::sort`

For sorting 10,000,000 finite `double` values uniformly distributed on [0, 1), **`std::sort` is the better choice** for practical performance in nearly all real-world scenarios. Here's why:

## Why `std::sort` Wins

### 1. It's Not Pure QuickSort
`std::sort` in major implementations (libstdc++, libc++, MSVC STL) uses **Introsort** — a hybrid algorithm that:
- Starts with QuickSort (fast average-case)
- Switches to **HeapSort** when recursion depth exceeds ~2·log₂(n), preventing O(n²) worst-case
- Falls back to **Insertion Sort** for small subarrays (typically ≤ 16 elements), where insertion sort has lower overhead

A naive custom QuickSort lacks these safeguards and can degrade to **O(n²)** on certain inputs.

### 2. Highly Optimized Implementation
Library implementations are:
- Maintained by compiler experts who tune for specific CPUs
- Use **intrinsics** and architecture-specific optimizations
- Occasionally include specialized fast paths for certain data types
- Compiled alongside the standard library with aggressive optimization flags

A hand-written QuickSort is unlikely to match this level of tuning.

### 3. Branch Prediction and Cache Friendliness
`std::sort`'s introspective strategy and small-partition insertion-sort fallback are designed to work well with modern CPU pipelines. A custom QuickSort with poor pivot selection can cause catastrophic branch mispredictions and cache thrashing.

### 4. NaN and Edge-Case Handling
Even though your data is finite and well-distributed, `std::sort` handles all IEEE 754 edge cases correctly. A custom sort may silently produce incorrect results if assumptions change

# Recommendation: Use `std::sort`

For sorting 10,000,000 finite `double` values uniformly distributed on [0, 1), **`std::sort` is the better choice** for practical performance in nearly all real-world scenarios. Here's why:

## Why `std::sort` Wins

### 1. It's Not Pure QuickSort
`std::sort` in major implementations (libstdc++, libc++, MSVC STL) uses **Introsort** — a hybrid algorithm that:
- Starts with QuickSort (fast average-case)
- Switches to **HeapSort** when recursion depth exceeds ~2·log₂(n), preventing O(n²) worst-case
- Falls back to **Insertion Sort** for small subarrays (typically ≤ 16 elements), where insertion sort has lower overhead

A naive custom QuickSort lacks these safeguards and can degrade to **O(n²)** on certain inputs.

### 2. Highly Optimized Implementation
Library implementations are:
- Maintained by compiler experts who tune for specific CPUs
- Use **intrinsics** and architecture-specific optimizations
- Occasionally include specialized fast paths for certain data types
- Compiled alongside the standard library with aggressive optimization flags

A hand-written QuickSort is unlikely to match this level of tuning.

### 3. Branch Prediction and Cache Friendliness
`std::sort`'s introspective strategy and small-partition insertion-sort fallback are designed to work well with modern CPU pipelines. A custom QuickSort with poor pivot selection can cause catastrophic branch mispredictions and cache thrashing.

### 4. NaN and Edge-Case Handling
Even though your data is finite and well-distributed, `std::sort` handles all IEEE 754 edge cases correctly. A custom sort may silently produce incorrect results if assumptions change.

## Performance Expectations

| Aspect | `std::sort` | Custom QuickSort |
|---|---|---|
| **Average case** | ~handled very well | Can be good with good pivot |
| **Worst case** | O(n log n) guaranteed | O(n²) possible |
| **Small partitions** | Insertion sort (no recursion overhead) | Often recursive (more overhead) |
| **Tuning** | Expert-tuned for target platform | Depends on your skill |
| **Maintenance** | Zero (library) | You maintain bugs |

For 10⁷ uniformly distributed doubles, both will likely run in **O(n log n)** with good constant factors, but `std::sort` will be **marginally faster or comparable** with far more robustness. The performance difference, if any, is typically within **±10%**, well within measurement noise.

## When a Custom Sort *Might* Be Preferable

Only consider a custom sort if:
- You can leverage **domain-specific knowledge** (e.g., you know the distribution allows bucket/radix sort gains)
- You are sorting into **pre-allocated, cache-friendly layouts** tuned for your architecture
- You can implement **Parallel Sort** (`std::sort` is single-threaded; a custom parallel implementation could win on multi-core)
- You have **extreme latency constraints** and have profiled/benchmarked a custom version thoroughly

For uniformly distributed doubles, **radix sort** would actually be the true performance winner here (linear-time for integer representations of doubles with careful bitwise handling), but that's a different algorithm entirely.

## Bottom Line

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

std::vector<double> data(10'000'000);
// ... populate ...
std::sort(data.begin(), data.end());  // ✅ This is the right choice
```

**Use `std::sort`.** It is faster or equivalent in practice, provably robust, zero-maintenance, and the difference is negligible compared to the risk of bugs, poor worst-case behavior, and wasted engineering effort from a custom implementation.
